headline: Petroline outage leaves the Red Sea bypass test unfinished
deck: Saudi Arabia's east-west oil line remained shut after drone strikes, turning the next Yanbu loadout and Bab el-Mandeb traffic prints into the physical test for whether the route squeeze is easing.

confidence.label: route squeeze persists through next traffic check

body: Saudi Arabia's roughly 1,200-kilometre East-West Pipeline remained on precautionary shutdown after drone strikes launched from Iraq's Maysan province, leaving the kingdom's Hormuz bypass unavailable while the next cargo evidence catches up. The line matters because the supplied BBC summary puts Petroline at about 4% to 5% of global oil supply, or roughly 4 million to 5 million barrels a day, as a working alternate route to the Gulf chokepoint. [E1] [E2]

The physical damage in the record is still narrower than the market shorthand around it. The supplied file says Copernicus Sentinel-3 frames published into English-language coverage showed scorched ground and smoke south of Medina, while a Reuters satellite still ran with follow-on wire coverage; it does not yet identify the exact segment holed, the barrels held in the line, or a restart schedule. [E4]

The Saturday diplomatic layer widened faster than the operating facts. Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and the GCC secretariat condemned the strikes, with Kuwait describing them as a dangerous escalation and pressing Baghdad to stop its territory being used, while Riyadh's stated posture remained no response at this stage and a reservation of necessary measures. [E3] [E5]

My forecast is a 58% probability that by the next dated check, 2026-09-13 at 18:00 UTC, public traffic or loadout evidence will still show a squeeze: either no confirmed Petroline restart, no clean Yanbu loadout recovery, or Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb traffic prints still being read as constrained rather than normal. The counter-case is simple enough to test: a Saudi restart notice plus ordinary Yanbu loadings or a clean Bab el-Mandeb transit count would move this from route risk back toward a repaired outage. [E1] [E4]

The claim should stay on physical flow. The supplied evidence supports a shut bypass line, visible damage, regional condemnation and an unresolved restart clock; it does not prove who ordered the drones beyond the reported Maysan launch point, nor does it turn every price move into a barrel that failed to load. [E2] [E3]

evidence_box.fragment: Saudi East-West Pipeline/Petroline remains on precautionary shutdown after Thursday drone hits; the supplied summary puts the line at about 4%-5% of global oil supply, or about 4-5 million barrels per day, as the working Hormuz bypass.
Saudi arabia says drones from iraq caused injuries forced oil pipeline closure

New Western first-print of satellite damage, a clean global-share number in a BBC lead, and a Saturday diplomatic pile-on including Kuwait on X via Iran International and a SANA/Qatar/Jordan/GCC bundle.
Copernicus Sentinel-3 frames published into English copy this window show scorched ground and smoke south of Medina; follow-on wire coverage carried a Reuters satellite still.
Kuwait's foreign ministry called the strikes a dangerous escalation and told Baghdad to stop its territory being used, according to the supplied Iran International / Kuwait MFA row.

dissent.argument: I put the persistence call at 46%. The record supports a precautionary Petroline shutdown and visible damage south of Medina, but it does not identify the damaged segment, linefill loss, repair clock, Yanbu inventory cushion or a measured loadout drop. A cautious operator can leave the bypass formally shut while terminals keep loading from storage, and the forecast condition is broad enough to count ambiguity as squeeze. I would need a confirmed restart failure tied to loadings, or a clean Bab el-Mandeb traffic deterioration, before treating the route constraint as more likely than not at the 2026-09-13 18:00 UTC check.
